description: Age-appropriate chore ideas mapped to Responsibility Pillars. Used by the public /chores/ideas pages and intended for future in-app suggestion features. appData figures are aggregated, anonymized Family Chores usage statistics.

ageRanges.label: Ages 5–6
ageRanges.headline: First chores that build confidence
ageRanges.summary: At five and six, chores are less about the result and more about identity: kids this age love being helpers, and short, visible jobs teach them that their effort matters to the family. Expect to work alongside them, keep jobs under ten minutes, and celebrate completion loudly.
ageRanges.parentTip: Pair every new chore with a demonstration, then let them own it imperfectly. A crooked bedspread made independently builds more responsibility than a perfect one made for them.

ageRanges.label: Ages 7–8
ageRanges.headline: From helper to owner
ageRanges.summary: Seven and eight year olds can own a complete job from start to finish — not just a piece of one. This is the age to shift from "help me set the table" to "the table is yours." Multi-step chores and the first simple routines (morning, after school, bedtime) work beautifully now.
ageRanges.parentTip: Resist re-doing their work in front of them. If the folded towels are lumpy, let lumpy towels go in the cupboard this week and coach the technique next time.

ageRanges.label: Ages 9–10
ageRanges.headline: Real skills, real standards
ageRanges.summary: Nine and ten year olds are ready for chores with quality standards — a bathroom sink that's actually clean, a load of laundry folded the way the family folds it. They can plan ahead, handle multi-day responsibilities like pet care, and start cooking simple meals. Weekly routines start to outperform daily nagging.
ageRanges.parentTip: Define "done" together, once, in writing. Kids this age argue less with a checklist than with a parent — which is exactly why routines with visible steps work so well now.

mostAssigned: Fold a full load of laundry

ageRanges.label: Ages 11–12
ageRanges.headline: Independence with a safety net
ageRanges.summary: Pre-teens can run complete systems: a full load of laundry start to finish, a weeknight dinner, the family dog. The parental job shifts from supervising the work to auditing the outcome. This is also the age where coins start teaching budgeting, and where recurring routines build the habits that survive the teenage years.
ageRanges.parentTip: Hand over whole domains, not tasks — "laundry is yours on Saturdays" beats five separate laundry chores. Domains build planning skills that single tasks never will.

ageRanges.label: Ages 13–14
ageRanges.headline: Adult-grade work, teen-grade motivation
ageRanges.summary: Young teens can do nearly any household job an adult can — the challenge is motivation, not capability. Tie chores to things they want (autonomy, money, screen time negotiated up front) and let natural consequences do some of the teaching. Paid-style chores and bigger projects keep the system from feeling babyish.
ageRanges.parentTip: Negotiate the standard and the deadline, then step back completely. Teens respond to being trusted like adults far more than they respond to reminders.

ageRanges.label: Ages 15–16
ageRanges.headline: Rehearsal for adulthood
ageRanges.summary: At fifteen and sixteen, chores should look like a preview of running their own household: budgets, appointments, car care, cooking from scratch, and being the responsible person when parents are away. The goal is no longer compliance — it's competence they'll carry out the door in a couple of years.
ageRanges.parentTip: Audit outcomes monthly, not daily. A teen who plans the menu, shops the list, and cooks twice a week is doing more development in four hours than a dozen small assigned tasks could deliver.
